title: backstage-reading-scraps-and-mini-summaries
content:
Purpose: very rough personal scratchpad to capture short summaries, concrete experiment seeds, and question threads I want to explore after skimming recent papers + two conference talks. Not polished — use as a journal and a place to drop ideas to revisit in weekly sync.

Quick index:
- Papers/Talks (short bullets)
- Concrete micro-experiments (what I can run on a dev GPU)
- Open questions / hypotheses / measurement plan
- Ops/infra notes (integration with KV cache + batching)
- TODOs / followups and people to ping

Papers & quick takeaways:
1) Sparse KV MoE for long contexts (paper: arXiv:2303.08774)
   - Core idea: route prefix windows to expert submodules to keep memory small while preserving retrieval for long contexts.
   - What I liked: clever routing + sparsity to trade compute for memory. Could be useful to reduce KV size for very long dialogues.
   - Limitations: extra routing overhead, potential QoS gaps for rare tokens.
   - Note to self: try simulating sparse-KV with a cheap gating layer on top of our current KV cache to see perf/latency tradeoffs.

2) Quantization-aware attention kernels (conference talk recap: SystemsConf 2029)
   - Key point: attention math can be restructured to maintain dynamic range at scale even when weights are int8/4 using per-head scaling and local residual compensation.
   - Practical: might reduce need for FP16 fallbacks for specific models; but requires kernel-level changes and careful FP->int accumulators.
   - Low-barrier experiment: benchmark one attention op using static per-head scaling on a small GPT-like model and compare perplexity/throughput.

3) Adaptive batching for tail-latency SLOs (paper + GitHub impl)
   - Idea: prioritize low-latency requests into smaller batches while opportunistically adding queued low-priority requests.
   - Implementation thought: integrate with request metadata (priority flag) in our serving runtime; fall back to cost-driven routing for non-priority.

Concrete micro-experiments (devbox-friendly):
- EXP-A: "sparse-kv-proxy"
  - Mock routing: for a 32k sequence, chunk into 1k windows, hash tokens to 8 "virtual experts" and only materialize KV entries for the top-2 received experts per request.
  - Metrics: effective KV memory footprint, hits on cache, end-to-end latency for autoregressive 1k token generation.
  - Success criterion: >30% KV memory reduction at <10% latency increase.

- EXP-B: "per-head-int8-attn"
  - Implement per-head scaling factors applied before quantization; test on 1.3B and 7B base models.
  - Metric: token-level cross-entropy vs baseline FP16, throughput on A100 and T4.
  - Failure mode: explosive degradation on certain heads (detect w/ head-level L2).

- EXP-C: "priority-adaptive-batcher"
  - Add a simple queuing policy with two lanes: low-latency lane (max batch size 2, timeout 8ms) and bulk lane (max batch size 64, timeout 40ms).
  - Measure: p50/p90/p99 latency, throughput, tokens/sec, and cost per token.

Open questions / hypotheses:
- Can we get KV memory scaling roughly proportional to unique-expert-count rather than sequence-length with sparse-kv (i.e., sublinear scaling)?
- Does per-head quant scaling interact poorly with rotary embeddings / norm layers? Need to test on a model with RoPE.
- If we prioritize low-latency traffic, how badly does batching efficiency drop for overall cost? Which workloads keep cost stable?

Measurement plan (simple):
- Use internal microbench harness (GH: redwood-inference/benchmarks/devbench) to run 3000 short-gen samples for each config; collect token latency histograms and token cross-entropy vs baseline.
- All experiments first on single-GPU dev runner; then replicate on a small Dedicated pool (2x A100) for more realistic KV/IO patterns.

Ops / infra notes (how this might touch our stack):
- Serving runtime hooks: need a pre-routing step (plugin) that can transform request -> expert routing plan and signal which KV shards to materialize. This maps to our smart-routing layer.
- Caching: ephemeral per-request KV indexes vs persistent backing store; consider LRU eviction per-expert.
- Telemetry: track cache-hit ratio per-expert, per-model-version; instrument request priority tags for adaptive batching.
- Rollouts: feature-gate sparse-KV behind model-version flag + canary rollout (10% traffic) with automatic fallback if latency > SLO_95.

Rough experiment checklist for next week: 
- [ ] Spin up EXP-A prototype (python) and run memory/latency sweep on 1.3B. (owner: Rhea)
- [ ] Add per-head scaling quant wrapper to quantization toolchain (owner: Mika)
- [ ] Prototype adaptive-batcher in local serving runtime (owner: Owen)
- [ ] Draft a one-pager for PM: short hypothesis, cost/benefit, recommended small scale pilot (owner: Rhea)

Conversation snippets / useful links to drop into the one-pager:
- Slack: #kv-cache (thread: 4/2 sparse-kv thought) — ping Owen for routing microbench
- Confluence: ENG-APPLIED/kv-cache-ideas (keeps notes on eviction strategies)
- Paper links: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08774 (sparse-kv moes), https://github.com/fast-attention/quant-attn (proto impl)

Loose heuristics & mental models I want to remember:
- Memory is a function of "materialized entries" not purely sequence length — if we can avoid materializing repeated/low-value tokens we win.
- Quantization tradeoffs are non-linear: small per-head tweaks can unlock big memory gains but cause rare-model breakdowns — need robust head-level diagnostics.
- Batching is a supply-demand problem: think of low-latency lanes as reserved seats. You give up some utilization for deterministic tail latency.

Notes to self:
- When writing the one-pager, include a small diagram: request -> router -> expert-resolver -> kv-store -> runtime (simple boxes).
- Keep initial canary traffic low and measure both latency and downstream correctness regressions (WER/perplexity on eval sets).

End of notes for now — want to iterate on EXP-A sketch tomorrow and produce a tiny notebook that can be run by an SRE on dev infra. If this gets traction, schedule 30m sync with Owen + Mika next Tues.

Random quick thoughts (scatter):
- Maybe we can compress per-expert KV entries using an LSH-style fingerprint to dedupe near-duplicates. 
- Could reuse our existing prefix cache APIs by introducing an "expert id" namespace. That keeps API surface small.
- Danger: more routing complexity = more opaque failure modes. Build strong observability early (per-expert error rates, size, eviction counts).

-- rhea
